meta.title: Who really said "The hurrier I go, the behinder I get"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Carroll. It is an anonymous American workplace joke, first printed in 1943 and credited to a truck driver named Bill.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The hurrier I go, the behinder I get'?
meta.ogDescription: A 1943 Detroit newspaper quoted a truck driver. Carroll, dead since 1898, was not linked to the saying until 1971.

answer.label: Not Lewis Carroll — an anonymous American joke from the 1940s
answer.authorDates: Originator unknown · in print since January 1943
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator, which has traced this family of sayings, states there is no substantive evidence Lewis Carroll penned it and that it appears in neither Alice book. The earliest instance it found is a January 1943 item in The Detroit Free Press quoting a truck driver called Bill — “the harder I work the behinder I get” — and the “hurrier” wording turns up in The Indianapolis Star in 1958, collected as a slogan with no creator named. Carroll died in 1898, and was not connected to the joke until 1971.

source.heading: Where it actually starts

source.excerpt:
“Ya gettin’ caught up with your work, Bill?”
“Naw,” replied Bill, dejectedly, “the harder I work the behinder I get.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s article ↗ is the anchor: “There is no substantive evidence that Lewis Carroll penned this saying; it does not appear in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland or Through the Looking-Glass.” QI dates the family to January 1943 and the “hurrier” form to November 1958, and concludes the originator remains uncertain.

We downloaded the Project Gutenberg texts of ten of Carroll’s English books — 2.41 million characters — Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland ↗ (in two editions), Through the Looking-Glass ↗, The Hunting of the Snark, Phantasmagoria and Other Poems, Three Sunsets and Other Poems, Sylvie and Bruno, Sylvie and Bruno Concluded, A Tangled Tale, The Game of Logic and Symbolic Logic — flattened every line break so no phrase could hide across a line ending, and searched the lot. “behinder”, “hurrier” and “hurrieder” occur zero times — and these are invented words, so a near-miss is not possible. If Carroll had coined “behinder”, it would be in the books that made him famous for coining words.

A site-wide insource: search of Wikiquote — which reads the raw wikitext of every page — returns zero pages containing “behinder”. It is not on Carroll’s page ↗, not on the Wonderland page ↗, and not filed as a misattribution anywhere on the site. Nobody has debunked it there; nobody has sourced it there either.

The reason it feels Carrollian is that he wrote something adjacent, and QI catches the moment of confusion: a 1971 sports column put “The faster I run, the behinder I get” into Alice’s mouth and then answered it with the Red Queen. The real passage, in chapter two of Through the Looking-Glass ↗, runs: “A slow sort of country!” said the Queen. “Now, here, you see, it takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place. If you want to get somewhere else, you must run at least twice as fast as that!” Same complaint, entirely different words — and Alice never says the joke.
source.excerptNote: Quote Investigator’s transcription of the earliest instance it located — an overheard exchange between two truck drivers, passed on to the paper by a clerical worker at the Michigan Central Terminal. The “hurrier” wording this page is about comes fifteen years later.

author.name: Lewis Carroll
author.heading: About the name on the mug
author.bio: Charles Lutwidge Dodgson — Lewis Carroll on the title page — taught mathematics at Christ Church, Oxford for most of his adult life, and wrote the two Alice books and a shelf of logic puzzles alongside it. His real sentences are odd in a particular way: precise, deadpan, and usually about the rules of language rather than about how you feel. That is worth knowing, because the lines invented for him are almost always the opposite — warm, encouraging, and about you.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Carroll gets the credit, and then three of his characters get the line put in their mouths. None of it holds.

items.why: QI finds no substantive evidence ↗ for it, and “behinder” occurs in none of the ten Carroll books we searched. He died in 1898; the joke first appears in print in 1943.
A 1984 newspaper column attached it to the White Rabbit, and QI reports ↗ that a 2021 Guardian piece found commemorative coins printed with it as his. He says nothing of the kind in either book.
A 1976 column about school finances “through the looking glass” had the March Hare whisper it, per QI ↗. The March Hare’s actual dialogue is the tea-party scene, and does not include it.

Bennett Cerf filed it that way in 1965 and a 1975 anthology repeated it, both logged by QI ↗. That is a plausible home for the grammar, and it is honest about there being no author — but it is a folk attribution, not a source.

misattribution.truthLine: Plainly: the words are in neither Alice book, the oldest trace is a truck driver quoted in a Detroit paper in 1943 ↗, and what people are half-remembering from Carroll is the Red Queen telling Alice it takes all the running you can do to keep in the same place.

context.heading: Why it sounds like him
lead: This is the most understandable of the Carroll fakes, because the joke really is in Carroll — just not the words. The Red Queen’s running lesson in Through the Looking-Glass is the same complaint about effort that outruns progress, and “behinder” is exactly the kind of ungrammatical coinage he liked. Two true things about his writing, combining into one false thing about his writing.

You can watch the join happen. In 1971 a sports columnist wrote a Wonderland pastiche, gave Alice the modern joke, and answered her with the Red Queen’s real argument. Once the two are printed side by side, it takes one careless reprint to lose the seam.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology: January 1943, two truck drivers overheard in Detroit; December 1943, a Gatlinburg shoemaker; 1958, “the hurrier I go, the behinder I get” collected as a slogan in Indianapolis; 1959, a Chattanooga editor insisting he said “hurrieder”; 1965, Bennett Cerf filing it as Pennsylvania Dutch; 1971, Alice; 1976, the March Hare; 1984, the White Rabbit.

The variants are the giveaway. A written line stays fixed; a spoken joke mutates — harder/hurrier/hurrieder/faster, work/go/run — and this one mutates freely for fifteen years before anyone thinks to attach a famous name to it.
context.pull: The joke really is in Carroll. The words are from a Detroit loading dock.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI states there is no substantive evidence that Lewis Carroll penned the saying and that it does not appear in either Alice book; it dates the earliest "behinder" match to The Detroit Free Press, 30 January 1943, and the earliest "hurrier" instance to The Indianapolis Star, 23 November 1958.

QI documents the 1965 Bennett Cerf "Pennsylvania Dutch" filing, the 1971 column that put the joke in Alice’s mouth, the 1976 March Hare attribution and the 1984 White Rabbit attribution, and reports a 2021 Guardian piece about coins carrying it as the White Rabbit’s.

The full text of Through the Looking-Glass contains no occurrence of "behinder", "hurrier" or "hurrieder", and does contain the Red Queen’s "it takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place" passage in chapter two.
The full text of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland contains no occurrence of "behinder", "hurrier" or "hurrieder".
Carroll's Wikiquote page does not list this saying in its sourced or Misattributed sections.
